title: Back after leaving: permanent staff who return on part-time temporary appointments
question: How many long-serving permanent employees stop full-time work and then reappear on the payroll as part-time temporary staff, in which departments and in what jobs?
finding: 473 followed employees worked at least two full years on a permanent appointment and were later paid as temporary exempt staff for 1,000 hours or fewer in a year, with no return to permanent full-time work; 248 came back in the same job class they had held. 254 were being paid this way in fiscal 2026, for 146,463 hours and $12.5 million. The most are in Public Health (91), Police (89) and Public Utilities Commission (53). 63 of the 473 were paid for more than 960 hours in a fiscal year of return. The Charter allows a retiree 120 working days or 960 hours a fiscal year, whichever is greater, so more than 960 hours is within the limit if worked in 120 working days or fewer; the payroll cannot say who is retired or how many days anyone worked.
how: City payroll file, fiscal 2017 to 2026, for names that pass the matching rules. A long-serving permanent employee is one whose main job was a permanent appointment with 1,800 hours or more in at least two fiscal years. A return is any later fiscal year in which the main job is a temporary exempt appointment with 40 to 1,000 hours, after the last full permanent year. Counted by the department of the return; individuals are not listed.
limits: The payroll does not record retirement, so this counts people who look like returning retirees, not people known to be. On bringing a retired employee back: Charter section A8.511(c)(2) lets a retired person with special skills be employed “for not to exceed 120 working days or 960 hours, whichever is greater, in any one fiscal year and may be paid for that employment”, keeping the pension, and bars using the retiree to replace a permanent civil-service employee. The limit runs on the City fiscal year, the same year the payroll counts hours in. Because the limit is whichever of 120 working days or 960 hours is greater, hours alone cannot show a breach: someone working long days may pass 960 hours within the limit. Someone over 960 hours here may also simply not be a retiree, and other retirement plans in the Charter carry their own employment sections. Some of these people moved to part-time temporary work for reasons that have nothing to do with retirement. The retirement system’s records would show who is drawing a pension.
